Dear members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry.
My name is Abigail Perry, I am a resident of Starks, and I am submitting my testimony today as a farmer and vendor at the Farmington Farmers Market to express my support of LD 468 - An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
I am a small, family farm, who has been participating in the Farmington Farmer's Market for 3 years. The market has a PT, seasonal employee and the rest of the time, the info booth is staffed by other vendors at the market.
Last year, Farmington Farmers' Market customers bought $5756.59 of food with their SNAP benefits and used Maine Harvest Bucks to buy $2843 of fresh fruits & vegetables. Over the course of the seven years FFM has had an Info booth, customers have bought $30,562.15 of food with their SNAP benefits and used Maine Harvest Bucks to buy $18,254 of fresh fruits & vegetables. We had 60 new SNAP customers at market last year and 228 since 2018.
For my farm personally, the MHB and SNAP programs have allowed me to connect with new customers in order to get more local food in the hands of people who are very interested. It also provides a great connection to younger children, who can be so excited to have a few "dollars" of their own to spend at the market, on a bright orange carrot, or a big red juicy tomato.
It is so important to maintain the CONTINUOUS FUNDING at the $1.2 million level per year. That allows our market and others to plan for growth and expansion of the program without any funding uncertainties or interruption.

Dear members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry.

10035804:
Amanda Scarpone Poland LD 468
Amanda Scarpone Poland, Maine March 4, 2025
To Members of the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Amanda Scarpone, I am a resident of Poland, Maine, and I am a public health professional who works in the non-profit and philanthropy field. I am also a Board member of the nonprofit organization Cultivating Community. I am writing to you today in support of LD 468, An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food. As a public health professional, I know that equitable access to healthy, fresh food is a key part of Mainers having healthy and thriving lives. This bill would double the State Nutrition Incentive Fund and provide ongoing, sustainable, reliable funding for programs that benefit Mainers. This act ensures more accessible ways to connect Mainers with healthy, fresh, local food, and it ensures steady income for our own famers here in Maine. Farmers markets are a key part of thriving communities, and provide not just access to food, but a sense of community and pride and belonging. It is a place where our diverse neighbors converge and build relationships and this strengthens our communities. Incentive programs such as that covered in LD 468 boost local farmers' success (last year farmers markets led to $1.2 million in sales to Maine producers) and help our low-income families better use and stretch their budgets to provide fresh and healthy food to their families. This act also makes our communities more resilient and less dependent on the national food systems that are often unstable and also do not provide access to culturally important foods that our neighbors deserve. Maine is a state that prides itself on its fresh food, our farms, and our innovative restaurants. We should also pride ourselves on how we feed each other, and our communities. LD 468 helps us do just that. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 468.
Thank you, Amanda Scarpone

SUN Bucks, a new benefit program, gives families $120 in grocery benefits per eligible child to be spent on food, including fresh produce, during summer vacation. 10035878:
Brandon McDonald Presque Isle LD 468
Testimony of Brandon McDonald of Presque Isle before the 132nd Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry
Dear Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry,
My name is Brandon McDonald, and I am from Presque Isle. As a dedicated shopper at both the Presque Isle Farmers Market and the Micmac Farms Markets, I am writing to express my strong support for LD 468 - An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
My career in entrepreneurial development began by assisting small Maine microenterprise businesses in accessing guidance, funding, and support. This journey was significantly shaped by the stories of local farmers in Aroostook County, starting in 2016. From the late Leo Nadeau, a potato farmer renowned as the creator of Bub's Potato Chips, to the dynamic educators Tracy Roberts and Jan Grieco, founders of Great North Woods Teas & Herbs, I have witnessed firsthand how determined entrepreneurs utilize Aroostook County's Maine Federation of Farmers' Markets (MFFM) to launch, innovate, and test their business concepts without substantial financial burdens. Farmers markets across Maine have provided a safe and accessible environment for entrepreneurial experimentation for decades. In recent years, these entrepreneurs have achieved even greater success, progressing from a simple table rental at a local market to operating food trucks and eventually expanding into physical retail spaces and shipping beyond Maine.
While I am not an economist and cannot precisely quantify the financial impact of 15-20 vendors in a Saturday market on Maine's economy (for that, I rely on Amanda Rector!), I can confidently assert that a local farmers market acting as an incubator for 15+ businesses, attracting hundreds of customers each Saturday, and facilitating the sale of 100% Maine-made or grown products and services is a significant asset to Maine's economy. Smaller regional incubator systems often request nearly $1 million in funding to replicate the work MFFM markets accomplish at a fraction of the cost statewide. This is considering only the entrepreneurial ecosystem benefits of MFFM, not the countless other advantages, such as increased access to healthy, local, and sustainable agriculture.
The funding requested in LD 468 is a modest investment that will enable Maine's entrepreneurial ecosystem to diversify through the support of microentrepreneurs, many of whom establish thriving businesses by testing their ideas at farmers markets. I urge you to consider LD 468 favorably and vote for its advancement. Thank you.
10035835:
Brenn Thomas-Googins Patch Farm LD 468
Testimony for the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry in Support of LD 468 An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food
Sponsored by Senator Henry Ingwersen
March 6, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is BrennaMae Thomas-Googins and I am the owner/operator of Patch Farm in Denmark, Maine. I am a resident of Denmark, Maine. I am providing my written testimony today in support of LD 468. In 2016 Patch Farm (a small, highly diversified, certified organic farm) began participating as an Harvest Bucks eligible vendor at the Bridgton Farmers' Market. In 2017, during the Bridgton Farmers Market summer season Patch Farm had Harvest Bucks income of $245. Last year, in 2025, in the same 6 month timeframe, we took $1,233 in Harvest Bucks. In that time, much love and energy was brought to the program in our state - and that hard work, and funding has so clearly paid off! As the program became more accessible to participate in, in 2020 we began accepting Harvest Bucks directly at our farm through sales in our farmstand and CSA program. While we see the majority of our Harvest Bucks and EBT sales through the farmers' market, having those programs accessible at our farm offer our customers flexibility on when they can spend their dollars - no longer being locked into a single day of Farmers' Market (which oftentimes customers cannot attend due to other obligations). This has also helped to diversify our own income through these programs - as those customers find themselves able to attend our (open daily!) farmstand and spend those dollars.
It is always so fun to see a customer in line at the farmers market who has a special gleam in their eye, like they are just so excited to share something with me, or find me familiar in a way I don't quite understand. It's happened to me several times that when I finally engage in an interaction with them they say something like, "Oh! It's so good to meet you!" I smile back and generally reply with, "You, too!" and they follow up with, "I'm the one who always buys the spinach from your farmstand - I leave the harvest bucks under the tray?" and while I don't quite recognize the person, I do recognize just the very thing they speak of: the things they buy, and how they buy it. Often a conversation will ensure about how they are always driving by on Friday afternoons and how they realized that's the best time to get the food - and I get to explain our harvest days and we laugh a familiar laugh, having never interacted before in person - but in many small ways over their joy in the produce that we provide them. Often times we don't need to have in-person interactions to develop a relationship over food, and I love those moments at farmers' market, physically bonding with people from all walks of life over a bunch of radishes... but I also love lifting up the cashbox and seeing a handful of Harvest Bucks and knowing that spinach went to someone who really needed and appreciated it.
Additional state funding on the Maine Harvest Bucks program means these programs can continue to thrive - and we can continue to allow and support one another through food. I do know that we all need to eat, sleep and breathe for a living - and to ensure that we can help out that eating thing for everybody in this state, no matter their economic standing, is super exciting. The Maine Harvest Bucks program does that, and it's evidenced by the growth in Harvest Bucks spending, and the ability of farmers' like me being able to expand the opportunities to accept Harvest Bucks from just at a farmers' market, to being able to accept it through our farmstands, through our CSA programs. So consider supporting LD 468, it'll mean the world to a whole host of eaters.

Testimony of Shelley Megquier, Policy and Research Director, Maine Farmland Trust, to the 132"" Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry March 6, 2025
Good morning Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Shelley Megquier and I am testifying
today on behalf of Maine Farmland Trust (M FT) in support of LD 468, An Act to Address Food Insecurity by He/ping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
MFT is a member-powered statewide organization that works to protect farmland, support farmers, and
advance the future of farming. Our goals are to keep agricultural lands working and help farmers and
their communities thrive. Since our founding in 1999, MFT has helped to permanently protect farmland
in every county in Maine, amounting to nearly 57,000 acres across 345 farms. Our Farm Network includes more than 550 farms that have participated in MFT's programming either through an agricultural easement or through one of our programs. Our main program areas are Farmland Protection, Farmland Access, Stewardship, Farm Business Planning, PFAS Support, Climate Resilience, and Policy and Research.
Nutrition incentive programs in Maine, such as the Maine Harvest Bucks and Farm Fresh Rewards programs, play a crucial role in our local food and farming system because they strengthen access to local foods for community members with limited food budgets, while also contributing to the viability of
local farms and food businesses by helping them gain new customers and build sales. MFT regularly hears from farms in our network how much they get out of participating in these programs -- both
emotionally and financially. Farmers report that these transactions make up a substantial proportion of sales at certain farmers markets, indicating to us that the programs are doing what they are supposed to do to increase access to local foods for food insecure Mainers and to boost sales for farmers.
As background, MFT launched the Farm Fresh Rewards nutrition incentive program in 2016 and
collaborated extensively over the years with partner organizations operating the Maine Harvest Bucks
program to support the growth and reach of these programs across the state. We were thrilled to
partner with Good Shepherd Food Bank to transition the Farm Fresh Rewards program to Good Shepherd in 2022. These programs empower more Maine community members to support the success of our farms and align with strategies contained within Maine's Roadmap to End Hunger by 2030 to
improve nutrition security by supporting and sustaining a diverse and robust local food system.`
MFT supports LD 468 because it provides ongoing state funding for Maine nutrition incentive programs, setting them up to expand into more parts of the state and leverage more private and other public
dollars directly in support of Maine's residents, farms, and the broader local food economy.
We hope that you will support this bill and help strengthen food security in the state and boost sales for
Maine's food and farming businesses. Please let me know if I can answer any questions.

Testimony of Steph Grant of Washington before the 132st Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
Dear members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry.
My name is Steph Grant I am a resident of Washington, and I am here today as a Farmer to express my support of LD 468 - An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
Over the years I have vended at many markets around the state, the Bath Farmers Market in Bath, the Union Farms Market in Union, Pumpkin Vine Family Farm's Farmers Market in Somerville just to name a few and am currently doing the Rockland Farmers Market in Rockland. Most of these markets have been run fully by Volunteers, with only a handful having the ability to pay for an info booth person to handle the Harvest Bucks, Credit Cards and SNAP.
I have been lucky enough over the years to not only watch but experience first hand how much the Harvest Bucks program helps build up small communities. Harvest Bucks allows low income families to purchase healthy fruits and veggies from local farmers but they leave with so much more. These family come to markets and farm stand, they get to know their farmers, their neighbors and we get to know them. They come looking for food and leave as friends which helps strengthen our community.
My favorite example of how wide the impact of Harvest Buck is, is of a family in the next town over. They come to the market every week, rain or shine, to buy their groceries, something they would not be able to do with out Harvest Bucks. They know everyone by name, all the details about what's going on at whose farm, and we have watched these kids grow up over the past couple years. This family has become a part of our community, they are quick to step up when the market needs an extra set of hand, or a farmer need help, their oldest got their first job working for one of the farms who they became friends with through this market. A market they wouldn't have been able to go to if it wasn't for Harvest Bucks. Supporting the Continuous Funding at $1.2 million level per year of the Harvest Bucks program not only puts food on people's tables but gives them a chance build a bigger better community and the opportunity for more stories like the one I shared. You do not get stories, support and community like this going to a grocery store or box store.
My testimony here is purely about how wonderful it is to see these people and families come to farmers markets and grow our community. My farm does not normally receive Harvest Bucks directly since they are specifically for Fruits and Veggies. That being said we are still affected as Harvest Bucks shoppers still need their staple foods that aren't necessarily covered by. The money that comes into the farmers stays in the community which in tern helps us all.
Thank you for listening to my story and I hope to see continuous funding at the $1.2 million level per year to help feed people and grow our communities.

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. I am Sue Salisbury, and I represent House District 128, which includes part of Westbrook. I am here today to testify in support of LD 486, An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of this this important bill. When I signed on as co-sponsor of this bill, I had no idea what was about to happen at the federal level related to nutrition. Recently, the United States Department of Agriculture cut $660 million from the Local Food for Schools Cooperative Agreement Program in 2025. Another $500 million was also cut, which supported The Local Food Purchase Assistance Cooperative Agreement program, which provides support to food banks. These programs were the results of years' worth of research and data that show providing healthy food options not only increases the health outcomes of communities, but also helps local farmers get their products into schools.
Despite Secretary Rollins saying that these programs are "non-essential," we know that they are vital to keeping our communities healthy here in Maine. That is why continuing this funding and providing opportunities for Maine residents to access locally produced food is even more imperative.
Thank you for your time and consideration on this bill. I encourage you to vote ought to pass on this legislation, and I hope we can work together to keep this funding.
